item.title: Clinical KPI Dashboard and Digital Log
item.description:
Status

Not implemented

Problem

Laboratory records are currently maintained in physical logbooks and disconnected spreadsheets updated by multiple individuals. Searching for a specific record requires manually flipping through pages. Cross-referencing data across dates, analysts, or services is not feasible during daily operations. There is no single location to view current laboratory activity at any given moment.

What was built

An interactive Streamlit application serving as both a structured digital logbook and an operational KPI dashboard, with the potential to expand into a full operational LIMS. Staff enter records via an intuitive, comprehensive form interface; the application stores, organizes, and displays data, enabling immediate searching, filtering, and comparison without unnecessary page reloads.

Technology

  • Python: Backend data logic and application structure.
  • Streamlit: Interactive web interface for data entry and visualization.
  • Pandas: Structuring, filtering, and KPI aggregation.

How it works

  1. Laboratory staff enter daily records using a structured form on the web interface (service type, analyst, result, date, observations).
  2. Entries are stored and indexed so that any record can be retrieved by date, analyst, or service without reviewing physical pages.
  3. The dashboard layer aggregates entries into operational KPIs: daily volume by service, QC pass rates, and workload distribution among analysts.

Outcome

  • Metric: Fully digital logbook system — eliminates manual logging by multiple users and streamlines record searching and cross-referencing.

  • Impact: The laboratory would no longer need to maintain parallel physical and digital records. Data entered once becomes immediately queryable. Decision-making based on operational trends becomes possible without the need for manual report preparation. ### Evidence

  • Deployed at the Hospital MAC clinical laboratory.

  • Code maintained in a private repository.

item.title: AU480 QC Data Automation
item.description:
Problem

QC data from the AU480 analyzer required manual extraction and handling across multiple weekly sessions, consuming at least 2–3 hours of manual data curation. The process was repetitive, error-prone, and hindered consistent monitoring of analyzer performance. Any variation in manual handling introduced noise that obscured genuine QC trends. Since the operation relied on external infrastructure, there was no automatic local integration for internal data analysis.

Solution

A Python-based automation system that extracts raw quality control records, processes them through a Pandas pipeline to generate structured outputs, and automatically uploads them to the external analysis platform (app.cclabcontrol.com) using Selenium. This enables real-time performance monitoring and review from any web-enabled device.

Technology

  • Python: Core scripting logic, parsing, and data processing.
  • Selenium: Automated interaction with the database interface.
  • Pandas: Cleaning, normalization, and generation of clean, structured outputs.

How It Works

  1. Raw data is extracted from the local AU480 analyzer system.
  2. Records are loaded into a Pandas DataFrame and cleaned: inconsistent formats are normalized, duplicates are removed, and expected fields are validated.
  3. Selenium initiates an automated session and uploads the processed records to the analysis web app (app.cclabcontrol).
  4. The platform generates structured tables ready for QC review and trend analysis, eliminating the need for manual reformatting.
  • Metric: Processes weekly batches of over 100 analytes per day in approximately 1 hour.
  • Impact: Eliminated repetitive manual data handling. QC monitoring became consistent and reproducible: the same process runs the same way every week, regardless of who executes it.

Evidence

  • Active implementation in the Hospital MAC clinical laboratory.
  • Code maintained in a personal repository.

item.title: Clinical Data Pipeline: From Excel/VBA to Python
item.description:
Problem

Laboratory records were manually consolidated from multiple spreadsheets during each reporting cycle. The process relied on copy-paste operations, manual formula application, and formatting adjustments that had to be repeated from scratch every time. Errors accumulated unnoticed, and tracing their origins was difficult.

What Was Built

The workflow evolved through two stages. First, a set of Excel/VBA macros automated the most repetitive formatting and consolidation steps within the existing spreadsheet environment. As requirements grew and data volume increased, the process was rebuilt as a Python/Pandas pipeline that performs the same consolidation and cleaning tasks more reliably, scriptably, and maintainably.

Technology

Stage 1 — Excel/VBA:

  • Excel macros for standardizing formats and performing basic field consolidation across sheets.
  • VBA scripts to automate repetitive manual steps without altering the spreadsheet-based workflow.

Stage 2 — Python/Pandas:

  • Python scripts replace manual data assembly.
  • Pandas used for structured cleaning, validation, and transformation of records from multiple sources.

How It Works

  1. Raw records from multiple files are loaded into a single processing context (spreadsheet or script, depending on the stage).
  2. Formatting inconsistencies are detected and corrected: date formats, field naming conventions, empty rows, and column misalignments.
  3. A mapping is established between study codes and the common names used in reports to standardize the records.
  4. Cleaned and validated data is written to a single, structured output file for operational reporting.

Result

  • Impact: Reduced risk of manual errors during report preparation. The transition from VBA to Python made the process easier to audit, modify, and transfer—since the logic resides in code rather than cell references. - The metric for this project is qualitative: the value lies in reproducibility and error reduction, not in a single measurable figure.

Evidence

  • Both stages implemented at Hospital MAC.
  • VBA macros and Python scripts maintained in a private repository.
